source.title: Language-Pretraining-Induced Bias: A Strong Foundation for General Vision Tasks

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendix. It includes some apparent draft notes, but they do not prevent reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains GPT-2-based vision models on random image labels and reports training accuracy, but its cross-modality setup and language-pretrained initialization differ from the original standard-network experiments.
record.gate_note: Random-label training accuracies and test accuracies are reported in Tables 2, 4, 5, 8, 12, and 13. Reported convergence comparisons are qualitative or figure-based and do not give the time ratios or corruption-dependent slowdown required by V2. It does not test shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs, nor the effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation as specified in V3 and V5.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures fitting of fully random labels and performance across corruption levels in a new setting: language architectures adapted to images, with scratch and pretrained initialization. These results bear on V1 and V4 despite the paper's main purpose being cross-modality adaptation.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that language-pretrained initialization and a random-label bridge stage improve visual adaptation and downstream performance, and that updating selected early layers can preserve useful structure and reduce adaptation cost. High but imperfect random-label fitting is a reported result; they do not establish universal perfect fitting or the real-patterns-before-noise learning order.
record.recipe_differences: GPT-2-based models are adapted to image inputs; comparisons include language-pretrained initialization versus scratch initialization. The paper's bridge procedure is a cross-modality training setup and does not reproduce the original standard-network experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization (language-pretrained versus scratch) and which GPT-2 layers are updated affect random-label training accuracy. The paper reports different accuracy across datasets and random-label proportions.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-label bridge training improves downstream linear probing, retrieval, and cross-modality adaptation; parameter covariance and feature separability also change.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on random labels can modify representations in ways that improve subsequent supervised transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretrained initialization and updating early layers improve convergence relative to scratch initialization or updating later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization and the choice of trainable layers affect random-label optimization in image-adapted language models.

record.problems: The core results use a GPT-2-based vision adaptation setup with a changed input projection and language-pretrained initialization. Several random-label training accuracies are below perfect fit. Results for convergence timing are qualitative, and uncertainty estimates are not reported for these tables. The supplied text includes apparent draft notes and some table/figure irregularities.
record.rows_left_out: Left out the separate layer-update conditions in Tables 8 and 12, which report random-label training accuracies for all layers and selected layer subsets; the core full-model random-label outcomes and model/dataset comparisons are retained in Tables 2, 4, and 5. Also left out cited or qualitative figure-only outcomes without separately recoverable numeric values.

untested.parts: Generality beyond the tested image-adapted language architectures; guaranteed eventual convergence beyond the reported budgets. Random versus correct-label hyperparameter equality is asserted through a consistent setup, but complete random-label generation and test-label protocols are not detailed.
Training-time ratios for random versus true labels and slowdown as corruption increases. Faster pretrained-versus-scratch convergence does not establish either comparison.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs. The Gaussian-input covariance argument does not establish zero training error.
Behavior between the sampled corruption levels and direct separation of signal learning from noise memorization.

Necessity and sufficiency of the specified regularizers. Weight decay and drop path are present, but the sensitivity sweep reports downstream linear-probe performance rather than random-label fitting; dropout, augmentation, and removal of regularization are not tested as specified.
Within-training ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noisy labels. Separate label-condition curves and layer-freezing comparisons do not measure this ordering.

missing.what: Clean-label GPT-2 endpoints needed for V4: scratch/pretrained CIFAR-10 training 98.7/99.2%, test 86.0/87.1%; CIFAR-100 training 98.8/99.1%, test 58.0/60.4%. These establish that the sampled sweep includes zero corruption.

Additional random-label fitting results: GPT-2 ImageNet-100 training/test 94.1/1.5%; Chronos-t5 ImageNet-100 80.9/1.3%, CIFAR-100 92.4/1.1%, and CIFAR-10 87.9/4.3%. These are not declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: R17/R25 and R23/R26 duplicate results and should not count as independent evidence. Reported gains are percentage-point comparisons, not uncertainty estimates. The paper states a consistent Adam training setup with weight decay and drop path. Failure to reach perfect accuracy within a finite budget establishes a scope limitation, not inability to memorize with further training. No original-source exclusion applies.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses GPT-2-based image models and includes language-pretrained initialization; it does not establish the claim for standard deep networks generally or show that fitting occurs without changing architecture or training setup.
Reports 15%, 30%, and 100% random-label conditions, but not a complete sweep from no corruption to all corruption; the results do not show perfect training fit across conditions.

statements.correction: Table 5: Qwen3-8B 95.9%, 93.3%, 92.4%; Qwen3-14B 97.9%, 97.7%, 94.3%. Section 6: Qwen experiments use 8×A100 GPUs; Qwen-specific epoch counts not stated. Near-zero-error threshold unspecified.
statements.problem: The accuracies are correct, but the text does not specify dataset-specific Qwen training budgets; the two approximately 98% fits are nearly complete under the state rules.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Language-pretrained GPT-2-based models on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and the larger Qwen3 models
reader_labels.reason: Random-label training accuracy is substantially higher with language-pretrained initialization, but reported values remain below perfect fit (R13, R15, R17, R19, R21, R23, R25-R34). Scratch GPT-2 is much lower at 100% random labels (R5, R11). The altered cross-modality setup does not establish the broader claim of unchanged standard networks.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 15%, 30%, and 100% random-label ratios
reader_labels.reason: Training accuracy is not perfect across the reported corruption ratios, and the test-accuracy values do not themselves establish the stated smooth rise toward chance (R1-R24).
